New luxury serviced living brand Fraser Suites Reserve to debut in Bangkok
article:
Frasers Hospitality, a business unit of Frasers Property, has announced Fraser Suites Reserve, its new luxury serviced living brand which will include curated holistic wellbeing features.

The brand’s first property will be located in Bangkok, Thailand.

The 255-room Fraser Suites Reserve Bangkok — occupying the top 10 floors of a 45-storey premium office and retail tower at One Bangkok — will start welcoming guests from December 2026 under a phased opening.

Its grand opening is planned for March 2027, when the full range of facilities and experiences will be available.

As part of the new brand’s wellness focus, the property will feature a House of Rejuvenation — a dedicated environment for recovery and renewal, offering therapist-led treatments as well as advanced wellness facilities such as thermal pools, cold plunges, compression therapy, dry flotation and red-light therapy.

Guests will also have access to The Wellness Edit, Frasers Hospitality’s global wellness programme.

Fraser Suites Reserve is intended as "the ultimate luxury for today's global professionals", the company said in a Sept 22 release.

Its rooms will be designed to offer privacy and calm, with many to feature integrated kitchenettes.

Dining concepts, wellness and leisure experiences, as well as a private lounge will also be available at the properties.

"The experience is complemented by the discreet yet highly personalised service of luxury hospitality," the company added.

Chew Hang Song, chief operating officer of Frasets Hospitality, noted that the brand will provide an experience "that feels immediately familiar and deeply human, supported by service that is warm and intuitive, yet respectful of their privacy".

title: Lyf Chinatown Singapore pairs social living with heritage in city centre — what to expect from a stay
article:
[Note: The writer's stay was hosted by the property as a complimentary media stay. EdgeProp Singapore maintains full editorial independence over its reviews.]

For a visitor staying in Singapore for a week or longer, the 90-room serviced residence lyf Chinatown Singapore has much of what one might need within walking distance.

Chinatown MRT Station and Chinatown Point are just a four-minute walk away, while supermarkets, hawker centres, traditional teahouses, restaurants, cafes and bars are scattered around the surrounding streets.

The CBD is nearby, and Chinatown's temples, conserved shophouses and other heritage sites offer plenty to explore without getting on a train.

The location is one of the property's key advantages, especially for its target audience of travellers who are staying beyond a typical hotel weekend.

Opened in July, the four-storey lyf Chinatown spans a row of pre-war conservation shophouses and a newly developed building along Mosque Street.

It is Ascott's fifth and latest lyf property in Singapore, and incorporates references to the area's long-standing links with the Chulia community in its interiors, artworks and guest programming.

Ascott positions lyf as an experience-led "social living" brand. The concept shares characteristics with co-living, including personal living spaces supplemented by communal areas and activities meant to encourage interaction among residents.

Settling in for six nights or more

At the Chinatown serviced residence, stays are a minimum of six nights per booking.

Its rooms therefore have to work for more than sleeping and showering for a night or two, while facilities for working, cooking, laundry and recreation become more relevant.

Given its location in the heart of Chinatown, the social aspect extends into the surrounding neighbourhood through local collaborations, recommendations and activities such as a guided heritage walk.

I stayed at the property over several nights as part of a media experience, testing its rooms and facilities and getting a sense of how well the social-living concept caters to longer-term residents.

For me, Lyf Chinatown's central location, lively communal areas and vibrant, heritage-inspired design were among the highlights.

The planning and design of my room also made clever use of its limited space, with a handy ledge above the bed with ample charging points, blackout blinds, and a spacious bathroom with plenty of natural light. These were complemented by a well-equipped shared kitchenette just outside my door.

That said, the room's workspace, storage and soundproofing had some limitations that could become more noticeable over six nights or longer.

Chulia links to Chinatown's past

Lyf Chinatown's heritage references are closely tied to the history of the Chulia community in this part of Singapore.

The Chulias were Tamil Muslim immigrants from southern India's Coromandel Coast, who began arriving in Singapore in the 1820s. Most of them worked as traders and moneychangers, with many living in Chinatown.

The nearby Jamae Mosque, also known as Masjid Chulia, on South Bridge Road was built by the community around the 1830s. Mosque Street, which runs alongside the mosque, takes its name from it.

The wider development, which houses lyf Chinatown as well as retail and dining spaces, is built on wakaf (trust) land.

Lyf Chinatown is among the properties in Warees Investments’ portfolio, with Ascott engaged to manage the 90-key serviced residence under the lyf brand.

Warees is an endowment asset management company wholly owned by the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (Muis).

Heritage meets playful design

RSP Architects and interior design consultancy Farm were behind the development's architecture and interiors, which pair playful, whimsical touches with the sensitive conservation of its pre-war shophouses and references to the area’s history.

The area's Chulia heritage carries through to lyf Chinatown Singapore's commissioned artworks and design details, including references to the journeys of early Chulia traders.

Recurring illustrated motifs by local artists include familiar Chinatown imagery such as shophouses, lanterns, koi fish, fortune cats, roosters, as well as the Queen’s Crepe Myrtle — a flower native to tropical south Asia, including south India’s Coromandel Coast.

Entering from Mosque Street takes residents straight into Connect, a colourful and informal ground-floor space that serves as lyf's lobby and co-working area.

Criss-cross patterns throughout the property, including on lamps and walls, take their cue from motifs at the historic Jamae Mosque.

Inside the lifts, phrases in Singapore's four official languages — Malay, Mandarin Chinese, Tamil and English — add a multicultural touch, a nod to the diversity of the neighbourhood and city-state.

Whimsical illustrations mixing cultural and travel references appear in the corridors, shared spaces and rooms.

My favourite communal area was the outdoor courtyard, where large, eye-catching murals by local artists make it one of the property's most photogenic spaces.

These curated shared zones — including the courtyard, rooftop swimming pool, the 24-hour Bond social kitchen, Collab meeting room, and Unwind flexible space — give residents more options for where to work, relax or socialise. That can be especially useful for those with smaller rooms.

The heritage theme also extends to lyf's programming. A rotating line-up of activities developed with local partners includes traditional Chinese calligraphy, henna artistry, tea appreciation, Muslim-friendly perfumery workshops and local culinary experiences.

In addition, a 1.5-hour guided heritage walk takes residents into the surrounding neighbourhood. During the tour, a lyf staff member, an "Ambassador of Buzz", led us through Chinatown and shared more about the area's rich history, landmarks and lesser-known stories of its early communities.

How the room works for an extended stay

Lyf Chinatown Singapore has 11 unit types, ranging from smaller rooms for individuals and couples to larger apartments that can accommodate up to four people.

They are sized from 118 sq ft and 129 sq ft for the Nano Queen and Level Up units, respectively, to 377 sq ft and 441 sq ft for the All Together (Two-Bedroom) and One Of A Kind Plus apartments.

I stayed in a Nano Queen unit measuring 118 sq ft, with a queen bed, en suite bathroom and desk, while sharing a kitchenette with just one neighbour in a dual-key setup.

The kitchenette was designed for only one person to cook at a time, but it was adequately equipped with all the essentials for simple everyday meals during a longer stay.

A slim built-in table opposite offers some welcome extra surface area for preparing or eating a meal, and could serve as a small workspace too.

For heavier cooking or group meals, residents can head to Bond, the 24-hour social kitchen, which has much more space and seating.

Inside my room, storage was quite limited; there was enough floor space behind the door to leave a small suitcase open, although accommodating a second would have been difficult. The clearance beneath my bed was too low to be of much use for luggage. A safe was provided for valuables.

A low entryway shelf gave me a convenient spot to leave my bag and other belongings within easy reach.

As there was limited space for a bedside table, the ledge running above the bed was a useful alternative.

Besides providing somewhere to place my phone, earphones, glasses and other personal items, this ledge has three three-pin power sockets, as well as two USB-A and two USB-C ports. That makes charging several devices overnight easy without having to hunt for available sockets around the room.

I slept comfortably, with the air-conditioning keeping the room cool throughout the night. The mattress was a little too firm for my liking, but the plump pillows and soft comforter made the bed cosy overall.

Housekeeping varies by length of stay, with one light clean every three nights and a full clean every seven nights.

Workspace, storage could be better planned

With a minimum stay of six nights, residents may bring more luggage, unpack more clothes and spend some time working in their rooms.

This makes the in-room storage and workspace more important than they might be for a weekend stay.

The desk worked well enough for shorter stretches of work. The WiFi was fast and the chair comfortable, if slightly small.

However, there was oddly just one power socket, located right below the clothes rail. I could plug in my laptop, the table lamp or the electric kettle — but only one at a time. The latter two also took up some of the limited, valuable desk space.

There is no wardrobe, so the rail above the desk is the main place to hang clothes when unpacking for an extended stay. But once that is in use, less of the desk is free for other items, as garments can brush against anything placed below. Long dresses, skirts and pants are even trickier, as their hems can drape over or come close to the desk.

More dedicated luggage and clothes storage would have been welcome for a stay of a week or longer.

Thankfully, working from the room is not the only option. The Connect co-working area has larger tables and plenty of seating, while Unwind is a flexible space where residents can work, eat, relax or socialise.

If you prefer an open-air setting, the courtyard has outdoor lounge seating where you can work or take calls. As a bonus, its murals make for a far more vibrant backdrop for video meetings than a blank wall.

Remote workers who like a change of scenery or having others around may find themselves spending more time in these social spaces.

Those who prefer working in private or need to take frequent calls may find the in-room desk setup less suitable.

Comfort, natural light and street noise

The bathroom in my unit was unexpectedly spacious, although I would have been happy to trade some of that floor area for a slightly bigger bedroom.

Water pressure in the shower was excellent, while half-height frosted glazing brought natural light into the bathroom without sacrificing privacy.

A similar treatment on the bedroom windows let in daylight while screening the lower part of the room from the shophouses opposite.

This gave me a good view of the charming heritage shophouses across the street, and the blinds could be lowered for near-blackout conditions even during the day.

My third-storey, street-facing room did pick up some of Chinatown’s street noise, from occasional car horns and revving motorcycles to laughter and faint thumping from music at nearby nightlife venues on a Friday night.

None of it stopped me from sleeping, although light sleepers might prefer an apartment away from the road.

For me, the street noise was a manageable compromise for staying in such a central area. Restaurants, cafes, bars, shops and entertainment are a stone’s throw away, while several MRT stations are within walking distance.

Daily essentials and attractions at the doorstep

The location has much to offer both tourists and locals alike, with everyday amenities, dining, cultural attractions and transport connections all close at hand.

Chinatown Point mall has a supermarket and a variety of retail, F&B and other amenities.

Convenience stores pepper the streets surrounding the serviced residence, for snacks and sundries.

In addition to the many restaurants and cafes nearby, Chinatown Complex and Maxwell Food Centre provide a wide range of hawker food options. Ann Siang Hill and Club Street add bars and restaurants for evenings out.

Cultural landmarks including Jamae Mosque, Sri Mariamman Temple and Buddha Tooth Relic Temple are a one- to five-minute walk away.

Getting around Singapore is easy too, be it for locals commuting to work or tourists exploring Singapore. Numerous bus stops are close by, while the Chinatown, Maxwell, Telok Ayer and Clarke Quay MRT stations are within a four- to 10-minute walk.

Slightly farther away, Outram Park and Raffles Place interchanges are 13 to 15 minutes away on foot.

After several nights, I found lyf Chinatown Singapore to be best suited to solo travellers, couples, small families, remote workers and extended-stay residents who seek a central location and would like to use shared social spaces and communal facilities.

Its programme of activities also gives residents more opportunities to meet and mingle with others, while getting to learn about the neighbourhood and its heritage.

The combination of everyday amenities, transport connections and communal facilities works well for a stay of a week or longer.

With Chinatown’s heritage, dining and nightlife at the doorstep and several MRT lines within walking distance, lyf Chinatown Singapore works as a convenient base both for daily life and exploring the rest of Singapore.

title: Oil Prices Over US$100: 3 Singapore Stocks Most at Risk
article:
Recent surges pushing crude oil back over US$100 a barrel – driven by persistent shipping disruptions and global supply uncertainty – have reignited margin pressures across transport and energy-heavy sectors.
Energy producers
benefit when oil is expensive.
Companies with big fuel bills or weak pricing power get squeezed.
The real question isn’t whether oil is pricey – it clearly is – but which Singapore-listed companies are most exposed if it stays there, and for how long.
Why US$100 Oil Matters for Singapore Stocks
Higher fuel and energy costs raise operating expenses directly, and transportation and logistics costs rise with them.
Airlines feel this the hardest, since jet fuel is one of their highest single expenses.
Beyond company-level effects,
high oil prices
can feed into broader inflation and dent consumer demand.
The companies that come through fine are the ones with pricing power, being able to pass costs on without losing customers.
How to Identify Stocks Most Vulnerable to Higher Oil Prices
Five things matter:
Direct fuel exposure (how much fuel does the company actually burn?)
Pricing power (can it raise prices without losing customers?)
Hedging (does it lock in fuel costs and for how long?)
Margin buffer (how much cushion exists before costs bite into profits?)
Balance sheet strength
Oil sensitivity is about all five together – not just which industry a company sits in.
Singapore Airlines (SGX: C6L) – High Exposure to Fuel Costs
Fuel is Singapore Airlines, or SIA’s, single highest cost, and the current spike has already shown up in the numbers, even though the national carrier hedges a portion of its fuel costs as a buffer.
In the first quarter of its fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2026/27), SIA saw net fuel costs jump 78.5% to S$2.3 billion, which accounted for 41% of operating expenditures.
This caused operating profit to collapse 73.8% to S$106 million, at a 1.9% operating margin.
Most tellingly, SIA’s passenger load factor softened slightly to 87.1% compared to 1QFY2025/26’s 87.6%.
Can the airline pass on higher costs to passengers?
Travel demand has stayed resilient, which gives SIA more room than a weaker airline would have, and fares can rise over time.
But that takes months to flow through, while fuel bills hit immediately.
Furthermore, competitive pressure on key routes limits how fast fares can move.
The airline does have a solid cash balance of some S$9.1 billion, and significantly less debt, that provide real headroom to absorb the oil price pain for a while.
SATS Limited (SGX: S58) – Exposed indirectly, through volumes
SATS provides ground handling and catering services.
It doesn’t fly aircraft, so it doesn’t carry a direct fuel bill anywhere near SIA’s scale.
Its exposure to fuel prices runs through
its
customers and
their
volumes instead.
For the quarter ending 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027), SATS’s EBIT and EBITDA margins slipped to 8.0% and 17.3%, from 8.3% and 18.2% a year ago, because of inflationary pressures and disruptions to cargo trade flows and flight activity tempo.
The pattern is consistent with an indirect hit: When airlines fly less because of expensive fuel or reroute around troubled spots, SATS handles less cargo and fewer flights – not because its own costs spiked, but because its customers’ did.
Tellingly, SATS’s free cash flow (FCF) slipped further into the red to a negative S$22.6 million from a negative S$4.5 million a year ago.
This is a real but genuinely different kind of oil exposure compared to an airline – SATS gets hurt by other people’s fuel problems, not its own.
SBS Transit (SGX: S61) – The Transport / Logistics Operator
Here’s the twist.
A bus-and-rail operator such as SBS Transit, with a large diesel fleet, looks like an obvious oil casualty.
But it largely
isn’t
, because of how Singapore’s bus industry is structured.
Since the Bus Contracting Model (BCM) took effect in 2016, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) owns the buses and infrastructure, and pays operators a service fee that’s indexed to diesel and energy prices.
Essentially, LTA provides a natural hedge for SBS against diesel price risk.
The company’s residual fuel-price risk relates mainly to electricity, not diesel.
That said, given higher electricity costs experienced across Singapore thus far, SBS’s margins could face further pressure.
SBS is a steady, low-margin business.
Revenue for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) rose 5.3% to S$785.6 million on the back of higher fuel and annual indexation.
Meanwhile, operating expenses rose a tad faster at 5.6% to S$751.6 million on increased electricity tariffs and diesel prices, leading to a slight 0.3% decline in operating profit to S$33.9 million.
Unlike SATS, SBS still generated positive FCF of S$54.8 million.
Effectively, SBS’s potential offsets against higher oil prices are structural rather than pricing-based: The BCM fee itself resets with fuel costs, and a fully electric rail business carries no diesel exposure at all.
Beyond that, SBS also earns from higher-margin advertising and retail leasing services at its bus interchanges and stations.
These are small but genuinely fuel-immune slices of revenue.
Fuel-efficient buses help too, but only at the margin, since diesel costs are already indexed rather than absorbed directly.
What Could Investors Watch Next?
Track Brent and jet fuel prices directly, plus each company’s own hedging disclosures.
For SIA, watch the load factor versus the breakeven load factor – the gap that’s currently negative is the number that matters most.
For SATS, watch global cargo and flight volumes, not fuel prices themselves.
For SBS Transit, watch LTA’s statements on additional support and any lag in the indexation mechanism.
Across all three, watch management guidance and actual evidence of cost pass-through – not just the oil price headline.
But an oil shock isn’t purely bad news for equity investors.
Energy producers and select oil-service names benefit directly.
And if share prices fall faster than the underlying businesses actually deteriorate – plausible for SATS and SBS Transit, given their more limited direct exposure – that mispricing can become an opportunity rather than a warning sign.
Get Smart: Don’t Treat Every Oil Spike the Same
Oil above US$100 is a genuine risk factor for
Singapore investors
, but it hits companies very differently.
SIA faces real, direct pressure with load factors already below breakeven.
SATS faces indirect pressure through the volumes it depends on.
SBS Transit, despite looking like the obvious casualty, is largely protected by contract design.
Before deciding an oil-sensitive stock has become too risky, check fuel costs, hedging, pricing power and the balance sheet – and remember that a scary-looking industry label doesn’t always mean scary-looking exposure.
If oil eventually retreats, the companies that navigated the spike well should emerge with their competitive positions intact.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

title: Saudis tell Asian refiners they can soon pick up oil from Yanbu
article:
(Sept 22): Several Asian refiners have been told informally by Saudi Aramco they will soon be able to pick up oil from the Red Sea port of Yanbu, according to traders familiar with the matter.

At least three fuel processors have been given informal assurances about the loadings from executives at the state-run company, rather than official notices, the traders said, asking not to be named as they are not authorised to speak to media. No timelines were given, they said.

Loadings from Yanbu have been all-but-halted since the East-West pipeline, which was carrying about four million barrels of oil a day to the port, was closed after being attacked by drones launched from Iraq on Sept 10. Saudi Arabia was seeking to return about half the capacity within days, a person familiar told Bloomberg late last week, although there have been no recent updates from Aramco.

Some of the Asian refiners contacted by Aramco have already missed their scheduled loading dates at Yanbu due to the closure of the pipeline and have vessels in waters near the port or are heading there, the traders said.

Since the pipeline was attacked, the Saudis have increased exports to Asia from Ras Tanura in the Persian Gulf. This crude can be picked up via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman after it has traversed the contested Strait of Hormuz.

See also: India to buy less crude from Russia in wake of US threats — Bloomberg

European, rather than Asian, customers have been most affected by the lack of activity at Yanbu. Aramco told at least two European refiners last week that they would be allocated no oil under long-term agreements in October due to the attacks on the pipeline and that the decision applied to all of the continent’s buyers.

title: UK borrowing overshoots in fresh budget setback for Healey
article:
(Sept 22): Britain borrowed more than forecast in the first five months of the fiscal year, piling fresh pressure on Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey ahead of his debut budget next month.

The fiscal deficit climbed to £77.3 billion — £8.1 billion more than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) predicted in March. In August alone, borrowing came in higher than forecast at £18.3 billion. The OBR had predicted a deficit of £14.8 billion.

The figures highlight the challenges facing Healey as he prepares a budget that must both set out Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s economic vision while reassuring jittery bond markets than borrowing remains under control.

Burnham has set out ambitious plans from defence and devolution to housebuilding and social care. However, his room for manoeuver is highly limited, with the rise in borrowing costs partly triggered by the Iran war already estimated to have wiped out half his fiscal headroom.

Speculation is growing that the Burnham government will have to raise taxes to restore headroom to the £23.6 billion that existed before the Iran war and keep the faith of bond markets, where investors at one point this month pushed 10-year gilt yields to their highest in 19 years.

With households facing the prospect of a huge increase in energy bills as the Middle East conflict drags on, Burnham is under pressure to come up with further measures to help people with the cost of living. He has admitted that the upcoming budget will be “challenging”.

See also: China and US discuss AI, investment on second day of trade talks

title: Qatar sells US$3 bil in bonds as war sends deficit soaring
article:
(Sept 22): Qatar raised US$3 billion from its first public international bond of the year as the Gulf state contends with the economic fallout from the US-Iran war.

The deal drew more than US$7.7 billion in orders at the peak before bids eased to about US$6.8 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. They asked not to be identified as they are not authorised to speak publicly.

The government, which has seen exports of liquefied natural gas plunge and its fiscal deficit rise because of the conflict and effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, sold five- and 10-year bonds. The shorter debt was priced with a spread of 55 basis points over US Treasuries and the longer bonds were sold at 65 basis points. Both were about 30 basis points tighter than Qatar’s initial guidance.

The country issued US$3 billion of bonds in the private-placement market in April but had not entered the public market since November.

The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has hit Qatar particularly hard because of its reliance on the waterway to export LNG, by far its biggest source of export revenue. That revenue collapsed to just US$200 million in the second quarter, from US$9 billion between January and March, according to data from the ministry of finance.

See also: South Korea-US investment arm said to mull debut bond for US$350 bil pledge

Qatar is helped by being one of the richest countries in the world, with buffers including a US$580 billion wealth fund and more than US$70 billion of foreign-exchange reserves. It is rated AA by S&P Global Ratings, the same as the UK and South Korea.

Yet its economy will contract 12.1% in 2026, according to a Bloomberg survey of economists. That’s the worst forecast among all the countries surveyed by Bloomberg.

The budget deficit reached US$5.8 billion in the second quarter, equivalent to 11.4% of quarterly gross domestic product and the largest quarterly shortfall on record, JPMorgan Chase & Co economist Francesco Arcangeli wrote in a Sept 14 note.

See also: Global bonds recover as Warsh’s inflation fight calms market

Government revenue fell 57% from a year earlier, almost entirely because of the slump in hydrocarbon receipts, according to JPMorgan.

“We need a break” so the country — one of the main mediators between Iran and the US — can refocus on its economic agenda and diversification, Finance Minister Ali Al-Kuwari said at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday. “We hope there is peace, a deal.”

At the same conference, Qatari Energy Minister Saad Al-Kaabi underlined the importance of fully reopening Hormuz when he said Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, was “completely wrong” to suggest the chokepoint can be rendered irrelevant in two years. Bessent said it could be “a worthless piece of water” in that timeframe.

Some flows of oil and LNG are getting through the strait but only with the support of the US military and volumes of those and other commodities are still significantly down from before the conflict. There’s little sign that the US and Iran are prepared to restart peace negotiations soon.

Monday’s bond deal was managed by banks including Goldman Sachs Group Inc and HSBC Holdings plc.

The government of the State of Qatar is the underwriter of the Qatar Economic Forum, Powered by Bloomberg.

title: Higher costs of capital due to AI and fiscal risks could test financial system: MAS
article:
The surge in AI-related investments, growing fiscal pressures, as well as recurrent energy and supply shocks have resulted in a higher cost of capital, says the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) in their annual Financial Stability Review (FSR) on Sept 22.

The FSR is coordinated and prepared by the Macroprudential Surveillance Department of MAS’s Economic Policy Group. The FSR contains the analyses and results from the regular assessments MAS conducts on the risks and vulnerabilities that could affect the stability of Singapore’s financial system.

In their report, MAS notes that the capital-intensive nature of the AI investment cycle has added pressure to an already uncertain macroeconomic environment. Besides competing against sovereign bond issuances for investor capital, AI is putting a strain on semiconductor and electricity capacity, thus fuelling inflation.

In addition, advanced economies such as the US are facing rising long-term nominal and real sovereign yields due to higher borrowing needs, stronger investment demand, and higher-term premia.

Energy price pressures and diminishing supply buffers due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have contributed to the inflationary pressures as well. This is on top of trade policy uncertainty that is reconfiguring supply chains and raising business costs.

“A persistently higher cost of capital could test global financial resilience,” says the MAS. “Higher yields would raise sovereign debt-servicing costs, with spillovers to firms and households, while weighing on asset valuations. Abrupt shifts in interest rate expectations could trigger sharp asset repricing, amplified by elevated leverage, maturity mismatches and concentrated exposures, including in AI-related sectors.”

See also: Global reserves shift from dollar overstated, NY Fed study says

Even though AI has been a key driver of economic activity and corporate earnings globally, the MAS notes that an elevated cost of capital as well as increasing dependence on market financing will result in a higher hurdle rate for AI investment.

“A material shortfall in earnings or expected returns could trigger a broader reassessment of AI-related valuations, with losses propagating across public equity, corporate bond and private credit markets,” the MAS says. “Elevated leverage, concentrated exposures and existing redemption and refinancing pressures in private credit could deepen spillovers to the broader financial system.”

To assess the risks that a retrenchment in AI-related investments and energy supply disruptions could have on the economy, the MAS has conducted stress tests on Singapore’s corporate, household, banking and non-bank financial institution (NBFI) sectors.

See also: BlackRock, JPMorgan bet on EM as turmoil seizes global bonds

Overall, the tests show that most Singapore corporates and households have strong balance sheets that can withstand the shock on earnings, incomes and financing costs. Banks have adequate capital buffers to weather the downturn while NBFIs such as insurers and investment funds have sufficient capital and liquidity buffers respectively.

According to the MAS, robust earnings from local bank groups have helped to bolster their capital strength. Nonetheless, it adds that banks should still continue to maintain sound risk management practices and healthy provisioning buffers amid the uncertain macroeconomic environment.

Singapore’s economy grew by 5% in 2025, according to data from the Ministry of Trade and Industry, higher than most developed countries. Selena Ling, chief economist and head of global markets research and strategy at the Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC) previously told The Edge Singapore that AI has been a key driver for Singapore’s economic outperformance.

“If you look at the highest level of growth in the second half of last year and this year, you are really talking about the whole AI boom, and that has nothing to do with state backing or domestically-driven engines,” Ling says.

In fact, the AI boom and the insatiable demand for chips to power it has altered Singapore’s trading relationships. Taiwan, home of local chip giant TSMC, overtook China to become Singapore’s largest trading partner last year.

“If you strip out Covid-19 and the last few quarters where it was really turbocharged by AI, as a maturing and developed economy, typically if you look at the US, Europe or Japan, they are mostly growing by around 1% to 3%. That is usually accepted as what a mature or developed country can actually sustain,” Ling adds.

While economies with less exposure to AI could be more vulnerable to tighter global financial conditions, the MAS cautions that economies who are benefitting from AI will be exposed to the ups and downs of the AI cycle.

“Economies benefiting from AI-related investment and exports are better placed to absorb higher borrowing costs if strong earnings and investment continue,” the MAS says. “However, these economies are also more exposed to a pullback in AI, which could weaken growth and reduce their capacity to absorb shocks.”

title: NSE’s US$2.4 bil IPO gets subdued demand from retail crowd
article:
(Sept 22): National Stock Exchange of India Ltd’s US$2.4 billion initial public offering drew subdued demand, particularly from retail investors, as valuation concerns continued to weigh on one of the largest stock market debuts in India’s history.

The deal was subscribed 5.7 times and demand was mainly driven by institutional buyers who bid for 12.7 times their allotted portion, according to data on BSE Ltd's website. The non-institutional investor category — reserved for wealthy individuals — was subscribed 6.5 times while the retail investor portion was covered 1.3 times. NSE on Monday set the offer price at 1,785 rupees per share, at the top end of the marketed range.

The subscription levels fell short of other large Indian IPOs in recent years, another reflection of the valuation debate that has clouded the already downsized offering. LG Electronics Inc’s US$1.3 billion offering of its Indian unit was subscribed about 54 times in October last year while SBI Cards & Payment Services Ltd’s IPO was subscribed almost 27 times in 2020. HDB Financial Services Ltd’s offering drew bids for about 17 times the shares on offer last year.

NSE’s dominant position in one of the world’s fastest-growing capital markets and its high profitability drove a deal that values the company among the world’s 10 largest listed stock exchanges. But tighter regulatory scrutiny of speculative derivatives trading, a business central to NSE’s profitability, has emerged as a key risk that forced the company to scale back its valuation expectations.

“Profitability was one of the biggest concerns following the regulator’s crackdown on derivatives trading, a key source of revenue for NSE,” said Sandip Sabharwal, founder of research house Asksandipsabharwal.com in Mumbai. “At the same time, NSE was already widely held and actively traded in the unlisted market, meaning many wealthy and retail investors already owned the stock before the IPO.”

Proprietary traders’ share of equity derivative turnover has fallen to the lowest level in almost four years at the NSE as problems with the closing auction mechanism add to an increasingly restrictive trading environment, Bloomberg News reported.

NSE offered shares at 1,700 rupees to 1,785 rupees apiece. The offering consists entirely of shares sold by existing investors, meaning the exchange won’t receive any proceeds. At the top end of the range, the offering is set to raise about 226 billion rupees, trailing only Hyundai Motor India Ltd’s 279 billion-rupee share sale in 2024 among Indian IPOs.

At that price, NSE would be valued at about 42.9 times its earnings for the year ended March. While that’s a discount to domestic rival BSE Ltd, it’s well above the roughly 24 to 25 times ratio for some of the world’s largest listed exchanges.

According to Charlie Hong, chief investment officer of LOGOS Asset Management, regulatory headwinds surrounding futures and options trading, along with NSE’s relatively high valuation, may also weigh on the stock’s near-term performance.

See also: India RBI uses currency swaps to cut US$115 bil cash surplus

With lower than expected demand, NSE’s grey-market premium fell to about 3% on Monday from a peak of about 16% on Sept 7, according to ipowatch.in.

Before opening the order book, NSE allocated 67.46 billion rupees of shares to anchor investors. They included global money managers such as Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fidelity and Eastspring as well as sovereign wealth funds GIC and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. Among domestic investors, Life Insurance Corp of India, SBI Funds Management Ltd and ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co were among the largest participants.

title: Embraer nears regional jet order from Japan airlines in blow to Airbus
article:
(Sept 22): Japan Airlines Co is leaning toward choosing Brazil’s Embraer SA over Airbus SE for an order of about 20 regional jets, according to people familiar with the matter.

Japan’s national carrier, which has been weighing whether to order Embraer’s E2 or Airbus’s A220, is due to make a final decision as soon as October, the people said, declining to be identified discussing confidential information. A decision hasn’t been finalised, and circumstances could still change, they said.

JAL didn’t respond to a request for comment during the holidays; Embraer and Airbus declined to comment.

Should JAL settle on the E2, it would allow Embraer to deepen its ties with one of its biggest Asian customers and deprive Airbus’s A220 programme of another marquee client. The E2 has snagged high-profile orders from ANA Holdings Inc, Finnair and SAS Scandinavian Airlines in the past year and is in a competitive race to secure a large order from India’s IndiGo.

Bloomberg News reported in November 2025 that the Tokyo-based carrier was considering as many as 40 regional jets and 30 propeller planes.

Airbus has won A220 deals, including 150 orders from AirAsia in Malaysia. However, the carrier has faced concerns about its financial health as fuel costs surge from the US-Iran war, though the company has sought to ease such concerns.

See also: AirAsia asking Ares for changes to terms of US$200 mil loan — Bloomberg

Embraer’s standard E190-E2 jet can seat 97 passengers in a two-class configuration of economy and business class while the comparable A220-100 can fit 120 travellers. Both aircraft are powered by RTX Corp’s Pratt & Whitney turbofan engines.

title: Tencent releases AI image model to catch ByteDance, Alibaba
article:
(Sept 22): Tencent Holdings Ltd launched its latest and best image-generation model on the same day as rival Alibaba Group Holding Ltd kicked off its AI conference, signalling intent to catch up to industry leaders like ByteDance Ltd.

The Hy Image 3.5 Preview model offers a performance boost over its predecessor and is being integrated across Tencent products, including the Yuanbao chatbot and film-editing and design tools, the company said in a statement Tuesday.

The release shows Tencent accelerating its exploration of applications beyond text, while working towards its vision of building AI that performs tasks for the billion-plus users of its WeChat ecosystem. Meta Platforms Inc’s agent-centric Muse this week shot to the top of download charts on mobile app stores — underscoring interest in an agentic AI that can tailor content for users and help them carry out tasks like shopping and hailing rides. Tencent’s shares gained more than 7% in Hong Kong.

“Some investors are drawing parallels between Tencent and Meta, particularly given WeChat’s unique social ecosystem and its potential to support a personal AI assistant at scale,” said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

The Chinese social media and gaming conglomerate has lagged Big Tech peers in delivering boundary-pushing large language models. It recently hired former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu, who overhauled the company’s AI infrastructure and benchmarking standards. Yao, who now serves as chief AI scientist, has publicly criticised training models solely for the sake of leaderboard scores, saying Tencent will instead focus on product integration and solving real-world problems.

The company has also continued to attract top talent since hiring Yao. Tian Yonglong, a former OpenAI researcher specialising in computer vision, joined Tencent in July and now leads vision-language models under the Hunyuan team.

See also: Alibaba unveils AI chip to drive global data centre buildout

Shenzhen-based Tencent tested the Hy Image 3.5 Preview among hundreds of in-house designers, and said that the model achieved results on par with ByteDance’s Seedream 5.0 Pro. The new Hy Image model is slightly better than Nano Banana Pro from Alphabet Inc.’s Google and Qwen-Image-3.0 Pro from Alibaba, the company added. Tencent employs thousands of game designers and artists, who may benefit from the tool, though it didn’t quantify its quality claims.

title: New World, ADIA in talks for HK$3 bil hotel sale to UOL
article:
(Sept 22): Property firm New World Development Co is in talks to sell its 50% stake in a Hong Kong hotel to Singapore’s UOL Group Ltd, according to people familiar with the matter.

The potential transaction would value the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kowloon at around HK$3 billion (US$382 million or $487.4 million), the people said, asking not to be identified because the talks are confidential. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, which owns the other half of the hotel, is also in discussions to sell its stake to UOL, the people added.

The move marks New World’s latest push to bolster liquidity as the heavily indebted developer seeks a comprehensive fix to its balance sheet. The company was left saddled with debt following a yearslong property slowdown in mainland China and Hong Kong, and has previously explored options including an investment from Blackstone Inc — a deal which ultimately stalled earlier this year.

UOL and ADIA declined to comment. New World didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The terms of the deal are subject to change and the transaction may ultimately not be finalised.

The Hyatt Regency hotel is part of a broader portfolio New World was previously considering selling as one. The company held talks with Singapore-based Aravest Pte to sell its 50% stake in a portfolio of three Hong Kong hotels valued at around US$2 billion, Bloomberg reported in May. The portfolio included the Hyatt Regency alongside the Grand Hyatt and the Renaissance Harbour View Hotel.

New World is taking other steps to raise cash. The company recently secured approval to list a real estate investment trust in mainland China, which it projects will generate 3.24 billion yuan in net proceeds that it can use for debt repayment and general corporate purposes.

See also: Paramount said to settle lawsuits, paving way for Warner Bros merger

New World’s stock price has fallen around 19% this year, badly underperforming the wider market. It will report results on Sept 30, covering the financial year ended June 30.
